lessons.title: Retaining Lexical Scope via Function Closures
lessons.description: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the scope where it was created.

sections.heading: What is a closure?
paragraphs: A closure is formed when a function is defined inside another function and the inner function references variables from the outer function's scope. Even after the outer function has returned, the inner function retains access to those variables.
list: A closure = function + its lexical environment
The inner function 'closes over' the outer variables
Closures work because functions remember where they were created
This is not a special syntax — it's a natural consequence of lexical scoping

codeExamples.heading: Basic closure example
explanation: createGreeting returns a function that closes over the greeting variable.
Even after createGreeting returns, the inner function remembers greeting.
Each call to createGreeting creates a new closure with its own greeting value.
This is the power of closures — they preserve state across function calls.

practice.task: Write a function createMultiplier(factor) that returns a function which multiplies any number by the factor. Test with createMultiplier(2) and createMultiplier(3).
hints: Return a function that takes a number and returns number * factor.
The factor is captured via closure.

keyTakeaways: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from its creation scope.
Closures persist even after the outer function has returned.
Each invocation of the outer function creates a separate closure.
Closures are the foundation for many JavaScript patterns.
lessons.challenge: Write a function createCounter() that returns an object with increment, decrement and getCount methods — all sharing a private count variable via closure.

lessons.title: Data Encapsulation & Simulating Private State
lessons.description: Use closures to hide variables from the outside world — true private state in JavaScript.

sections.heading: Private variables with closures
paragraphs: JavaScript objects don't have built-in private properties. Closures solve this by keeping variables in the outer function's scope — completely inaccessible from outside.
list: Variables in the outer function are invisible to external code
Only the returned functions can access them
This creates true encapsulation — controlled access to internal state
This pattern predates the #private field syntax in classes

codeExamples.heading: Encapsulated bank account
explanation: balance is trapped in the closure — it's private by design.
The returned object provides controlled access via methods.
External code cannot modify balance directly — only through the methods.
This is true data encapsulation without class syntax.

practice.task: Create a createPasswordValidator(minLength) function that returns an object with validate(password) and getMinLength() methods. The minLength should be private.
hints: Store minLength in the outer function scope.
Return an object with methods that close over minLength.
The validate method should return true if password.length >= minLength.

keyTakeaways: Closures create true private variables — external code cannot access them.
Returned methods provide controlled access to the encapsulated state.
This pattern is used for validation, state management, and data protection.
Modern classes use #private fields, but closures work everywhere including older environments.
lessons.challenge: Build a rate limiter using closures: createRateLimiter(maxCalls, timeWindow) that returns a function which tracks calls and throws an error if the limit is exceeded.

lessons.title: Practical Closure Use Cases: Factory Functions & Memoization
lessons.description: Closures power common patterns — factories that produce customized objects and memoization that caches results.

sections.heading: Factory functions
paragraphs: A factory function creates and returns new objects each time it's called. Closures let each object maintain its own private state.
list: Each call creates a fresh set of private variables
Returned objects are independent of each other
Useful for creating multiple instances with different configurations

sections.heading: Memoization
paragraphs: Memoization caches the results of expensive function calls. Closures store the cache between calls.
list: The cache lives in the closure — invisible to external code
Subsequent calls with the same arguments return the cached result
Huge performance boost for recursive and expensive computations

codeExamples.heading: Factory function and memoization
explanation: Each logger has its own private count variable via closure.
The memoize function wraps any function with a cache stored in its closure.
Second call with the same args returns the cached result instantly.
Both patterns rely on closures to maintain private state.

practice.task: Write a memoized version of a factorial function using the memoize pattern. Test it with factorial(10) called twice to verify caching works.
hints: Add a console.log inside the factorial to see if it's actually computing.
The second call should not log anything — it's cached.

keyTakeaways: Factory functions use closures to create objects with independent private state.
Memoization uses closures to cache function results between calls.
Both patterns are fundamental JavaScript techniques powered by closures.
Closures make encapsulation and state management possible without special syntax.
lessons.challenge: Build a memoized async function that fetches data from a URL. Cache the result so the second call to the same URL returns immediately.
